teaching.rule: French has two pairs of vowels that English speakers tend to merge. First, u and ou: for u (tu, vue, sûr) say 'ee', then round and push your lips forward as for 'oo' while your tongue stays forward; for ou (tout, vous, roue) the tongue pulls back and you get a short, tense 'oo' as in 'food'. Second, é and è: é (café, léger, fermé) is a closed 'ay' held steady with no glide at the end; è (mère, fête, règle) is the open e of English 'bed'. The e sound is always open (è) when its syllable ends in a pronounced consonant, which is why premier ends in é with a silent r, but première ends in è followed by a sounded r. Swapping u and ou changes the word: tu / tout, rue / roue, dessus / dessous.

examples.note: The French u: say 'ee', then round and push your lips forward as for 'oo' without moving your tongue back. English has no such vowel.
The French ou: the 'oo' of English 'food', but shorter, with well-rounded lips and the tongue pulled back; the s is silent.
é is a closed, steady 'ay' with no glide at the end: ka-FÉ, not English 'ka-FAY-ee'. Smile slightly and hold the sound still.
è is the open e of English 'bed': MÈR. It is open here because the syllable ends in a pronounced r.

contrast.note: Only the vowel changes: tongue forward for u (de-SÜ), tongue back for ou (de-SOO). Mix them up and you say the opposite.
Both end in a vowel, since the t of tout is silent, so the vowel alone tells the two words apart.
The masculine ends in closed é with a silent r (pruh-MYÉ); the feminine ends in open è followed by a sounded r (pruh-MYÈR).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers replace u with ou, so tu sounds like tout and la rue like la roue, and they let é slide into the English diphthong 'ay-ee'. Keep the tongue forward and the lips rounded for u, and hold é perfectly still.

probes.en: only the vowel: tongue forward for rue, pulled back for roue
probes.ask: What tells “la rue” (the street) apart from “la roue” (the wheel) when you say them?
probes.ex: J'ai trouvé une roue de vélo dans la rue.
probes.exEn: I found a bike wheel in the street.
options: the r: rolled in rue, silent in roue
the final e: sounded in roue, silent in rue
nothing: the two words sound exactly the same

probes.en: on a steady closed é with no glide: ka-FÉ
options: on a glide, as in English 'day': ka-FAY-ee
on the open è of mère: ka-FÈ

probes.en: with the open è of mère and a sounded r: pruh-MYÈR
options: with the closed é of café and a silent r: pruh-MYÉ

items.note: The ou vowel: a short, tense 'oo' as in 'food', lips well rounded, tongue back (TOO); the t is silent. Keep it apart from tu (you), whose vowel is made with the tongue forward.
Rounded 'oo' with the tongue back (DOO), and the x is silent. It must not sound like du (some, of the), where the tongue stays forward for u.
The ou vowel with rounded lips (ROO). Compare la rue (the street): the two words differ only in this vowel.
The u vowel: say 'ee', then round your lips without moving your tongue (VÜ). With ou it would sound like vous (you).
items.ex: Cette chambre a une belle vue.
items.exEn: This room has a lovely view.

items.note: The u vowel with the tongue forward and the lips rounded (ZHÜ); the s is silent. Said with ou, it becomes joue (cheek; plays).
items.ex: Un jus d'orange, s'il vous plaît.

items.note: The u vowel followed by a sounded r (SÜR). The circumflex changes nothing in speech, so sûr sounds exactly like sur (on); with ou it would become sourd (deaf).
Two closed é sounds, lé-JÉ: the final -er is said é and its r is silent. The feminine légère ends in open è plus a sounded r: lé-JÈR.
Open è twice, with both r's sounded: dèr-NYÈR. The masculine dernier ends in closed é with a silent r: dèr-NYÉ.
ê is the open è of English 'bed' (FÈT), and the t is pronounced because an -e follows it. Do not close it to é. Faire la fête means to party.
items.ex: On fait la fête ce soir !

items.note: Both kinds of e in one word: closed é first, then open è before the v: é-LÈV. The final -e is silent.
Open è, then closed é: fèr-MÉ. The first e is open because its syllable ends in r. Without the accent, ferme (farm; closes) ends on the open sound: FÈRM.
items.ex: Le magasin est fermé le dimanche.
items.exEn: The shop is closed on Sundays.

items.note: è before two consonants is open: RÈGL, with the final -e silent. Règle also means a ruler for drawing lines.

teaching.rule: English stresses one syllable inside each word (ba-NA-na, PHAR-ma-cy, IN-ter-est-ing) and shrinks the others to 'uh'. French does not. Every syllable gets about the same length and a full vowel (the one exception is the light e of je, le or ne, which is often dropped in speech), and only the last pronounced syllable of a group of words is lengthened: cho-co-LA, un-ca-FÉ. A group is a chunk said in one breath, usually a noun with its article and adjectives, or a short verb phrase, so the stress moves to the end as the group grows: un café, then un café CRÈME. A final silent -e does not count, so in banane the stress falls on -nane. The stressed syllable is mostly longer, not louder: keep the syllables before it full and even instead of swallowing them.

examples.note: Three even beats, the last one longer: cho-co-LA, with the t silent. English squeezes the word into CHOC-lit.
One group said as one smooth stream, ja-bi-ta-pa-RI: no word inside it gets its own stress, only the very last syllable.
Four words, one group, one stress at the end, on vin. Verre sits in the middle of the group, so it stays light.

contrast.note: English says PA-ris; French says pa-RI, with even syllables and the weight on the last one. The s is silent.
On its own, café takes the stress on -fé; add crème and the group gets longer, so the stress moves to crème and -fé goes light.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers stress words near the front (PHAR-ma-cie, IN-té-res-sant) and reduce the other vowels to 'uh'; keep every syllable even and full, except the light e of je, le or ne, and lean only on the last syllable of the group.

probes.ask: Where does the stress fall in “Paris”, said on its own?
probes.ex: J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans.
probes.exEn: I've lived in Paris for two years.
options: on the first syllable, with the s pronounced: PA-riss
on the last syllable, with the s pronounced: pa-RISS

probes.ask: Where does the stress fall in “Je ne comprends pas”?

probes.en: on crème, the end of the group
probes.ask: In “un café crème”, which part carries the stress?
options: on ca-, the start of café

items.note: On its own, chocolat is stressed on -lat; add chaud and the group gets longer, so the stress moves to the end: cho-co-la-CHO, with -lat now light.
Two syllables, ba-NANN: the final -e is silent, so the stress lands on -nane. Both a's are the same open 'a', never the 'buh' of English 'banana'.
Four even beats, in-té-ré-SAN, with only the last one lengthened. English stresses the first syllable of 'interesting'; in French in- stays light.
Four even syllables with the weight on the final nasal: ab-so-lu-MAN. Do not lean on ab- as in English 'AB-solutely'.
Three even beats, dik-syo-NÈR, with the stress on the last one and the final -e silent. English stresses DIC-tionary.
One group, one stress at the end: un-nor-di-na-teur-por-TABL. Said alone, ordinateur ends on -teur; inside this group -teur goes light and the stress moves to -table.
items.ex: Mon ordinateur portable est trop lent.

items.note: Said in four beats because the e before -ment drops: ma-leu-reuz-MAN, with the stress at the very end. The h is silent.
far-ma-SI: three even syllables, the last one lengthened. English puts the weight on PHAR-; French keeps it light. In la pharmacie de la gare the stress moves on to gare, and -cie goes light.
items.ex: Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
items.exEn: Is there a chemist's near here?

items.note: Four even beats, la-ni-vèr-SÈR: the stress is on -saire, and the final -e is silent. In l'anniversaire de Paul the group grows and the stress moves to Paul.
é-vi-da-MAN: the -emment ending is said like -amment, and the stress sits on the last syllable only.
Three words, one rhythm group, one stress at the end: un-vèr-DO. Verre is in the middle of the group, so it is not stressed.
items.ex: Je voudrais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I'd like a glass of water, please.

items.note: su-pèr-mar-CHÉ: four even beats. English stresses SU-permarket; French leans only on the final -ché. In le supermarché du coin the group grows, so the stress moves to coin.
items.ex: Je fais les courses au supermarché.
items.exEn: I do the shopping at the supermarket.

teaching.rule: Where English says 'I am' plus a bodily feeling, French says 'I have' plus a noun: j'ai faim (I'm hungry, literally 'I have hunger'), j'ai soif, j'ai chaud, j'ai froid, j'ai peur. Age works the same way, j'ai trente ans (I'm thirty), and in a full sentence the word ans must be said. So does being right or wrong, avoir raison and avoir tort, and two very common expressions take de before what follows: avoir besoin de (to need) and avoir envie de (to feel like). Conjugate avoir for the subject (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont) and leave the word after it as it is: it never agrees, so elle a froid, not 'elle a froide'. To say 'very', add très: j'ai très faim.

examples.note: Literally 'I have hunger': faim is a noun, so French uses avoir where English uses 'to be'.
Age is something you have, and in a full sentence ans (years) is required: never just 'il a vingt-cinq'.
Being right is having reason: avoir raison. Its opposite is avoir tort.

contrast.note: For the weather use faire: il fait froid. For a person feeling the cold use avoir: j'ai froid.
avoir tort is for a person who is mistaken; for a statement or an answer that is incorrect, say c'est faux.

teaching.commonMistake: Once avoir is in place, learners still treat the word after it as an adjective and make it agree: 'elle a froide', 'ils ont chauds'; faim, soif, froid, chaud and peur never change here. They also drop ans from an age in a full sentence ('il a trente') and use avoir tort for a wrong answer, which is c'est faux.

probes.ex: Tu as besoin d'aide avec ta valise ?
probes.exEn: Do you need help with your suitcase?

items.note: Hunger is something you have: tu as faim, literally 'you have hunger'. Never 'tu es faim'.
Like faim, soif is a noun, so it follows avoir: j'ai soif. Add très for 'very': j'ai très soif.
items.ex: J'ai soif, tu as de l'eau ?
items.exEn: I'm thirsty, do you have any water?

items.note: A person feeling hot is j'ai chaud. Chaud does not change for the speaker, so a woman also says j'ai chaud.
items.ex: Ouvre la fenêtre, j'ai trop chaud.
items.exEn: Open the window, I'm too hot.

items.note: ont is the ils/elles form of avoir. 'Ils sont froids' would describe them as cold to the touch or unfriendly, not as feeling cold.
What you are afraid of follows de, and de + les becomes des: elle a peur des chiens.
Literally 'to have reason'. It works for any subject: tu as raison, ils ont raison.
items.ex: Tu as raison, c'est trop cher.

items.note: Use it for a person who is mistaken. For a wrong answer or a false statement, say c'est faux.
items.ex: Je crois que tu as tort.

items.note: The thing you need follows de, which shortens to d' before a vowel: j'ai besoin d'un café.
A softer way to say you want something: j'ai envie d'une glace, or with a verb, j'ai envie de dormir.
items.exEn: I feel like an ice cream.

items.note: à + the body part with le, la or les, not 'my': j'ai mal à la tête, j'ai mal au dos, j'ai mal aux dents.
Age takes avoir, and the word ans must be said: mon frère a trente ans, never 'mon frère est trente'.
Literally 'to have some luck', with the partitive de la: here chance means luck. A very common reaction to good news.

teaching.rule: Il faut says that something is necessary without saying who has to do it. Its il stands for nobody, so it never changes: there is no 'je faut' or 'on faut'. Follow it with an infinitive for an action, il faut partir, and English picks 'we', 'you' or 'one' from the situation. Follow it with a noun for what is needed or for how long something takes: il faut un passeport (you need a passport), il faut deux heures (it takes two hours). To say who needs a thing, put a pronoun before faut: il me faut un stylo (I need a pen). The negative il ne faut pas forbids (you mustn't); the future is il faudra. Il faut que + a full clause also exists, but it needs the subjunctive, which comes later.

examples.note: faut + infinitive, no de in between. The il is impersonal, and English chooses 'we' because of the situation.

examples.fr: Il faut deux heures en train.
examples.en: It takes two hours by train.
examples.note: With a length of time, il faut translates 'it takes'.

examples.fr: Il nous faut une plus grande table.
examples.note: A pronoun before faut (me, te, nous, vous) names who needs the thing.

contrast.fr: Il ne faut pas venir. / Tu n'as pas besoin de venir.
contrast.en: You mustn't come. / You don't have to come.
contrast.note: il ne faut pas forbids; it does not mean 'you don't have to'. For that, use pas besoin de or ce n'est pas la peine de.

contrast.fr: Il faut partir. / Il doit partir.
contrast.en: We have to leave. / He has to leave.
contrast.note: With devoir, il is a real person (he). With faut, il is nobody, and the person comes from the context.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers read il faut as 'he needs' or build 'je faut'; faut only ever takes impersonal il. They also use il ne faut pas for 'you don't have to', when it actually means 'you mustn't'.

probes.ex: Il ne faut pas courir dans le couloir.
probes.exEn: You mustn't run in the corridor.

probes.fr: Il faut dix minutes à pied.
probes.en: It takes ten minutes on foot.
probes.ex: Pour aller à la gare, il faut dix minutes à pied.
probes.exEn: It takes ten minutes on foot to get to the station.
options: He needs ten minutes on foot.

probes.ex: Pour ce gâteau, il me faut du sucre.
probes.exEn: I need some sugar for this cake.

items.note: il faut + infinitive: the il is nobody in particular, and English chooses 'we', 'you' or 'I' from the situation.
items.ex: Il est tard, il faut partir.
items.exEn: It's late, we have to leave.

items.note: No de and no que between faut and the infinitive: il faut réserver, not 'il faut de réserver'.
items.ex: Le restaurant est petit, il faut réserver.
items.exEn: The restaurant is small, you need to book.

items.note: ne and pas go around faut. This forbids something; it never means 'you don't have to'.
items.ex: Il ne faut pas fumer ici.

items.note: With a length of time, il faut means 'it takes'. Ça prend deux heures is a more casual equivalent.
items.ex: D'ici, il faut deux heures en train.
items.exEn: From here, it takes two hours by train.

items.note: me before faut says who needs the thing. The il is still impersonal: il me faut never means 'he needs'.
items.ex: Il me faut un stylo, tu en as un ?
items.exEn: I need a pen, do you have one?

items.en: what do we need to bring?
items.note: qu'est-ce qu'il faut + infinitive asks what has to be done, without naming who does it.
items.ex: Pour le pique-nique, qu'est-ce qu'il faut apporter ?
items.exEn: What do we need to bring for the picnic?

items.note: être stays in the infinitive after faut: il faut être, never 'il faut est'.
items.ex: Avec les enfants, il faut être patient.
items.exEn: With children, you have to be patient.

items.note: il faut + a noun says what is needed, with its article: il faut un passeport, il faut du temps.
items.ex: Pour ce voyage, il faut un passeport.
items.exEn: You need a passport for this trip.

items.note: In conversation the question word can sit after faut. Combien de temps faut-il ? is the more formal order.
items.ex: Il faut combien de temps pour aller à la gare ?
items.exEn: How long does it take to get to the station?

items.note: nous before faut says who needs the thing; the il stays impersonal. Nous avons besoin de and on a besoin de say the same.
items.ex: Il nous faut deux chambres pour ce soir.
items.exEn: We need two rooms for tonight.

items.note: il faut + du temps: the partitive du because time is uncountable here. Ça prend du temps is a more casual equivalent.
items.ex: Pour apprendre une langue, il faut du temps.
